# Effect Size Summary

d = -0.25, 95% CI [-0.4, -0.1] based on N = 730.


# Summary of Analysis Approach

We analysed data from UK Psychology undergraduates with university-reported statistics module grades who passed relevant attention checks. Statistics anxiety was measured using the total score of the 23 Statistics Anxiety Rating Scale (STARS) questions. Our main analysis examined the relationship between total STARS score and statistics module grade (%), explored using Pearson's correlation coefficient, converted to Cohen's d. To investigate the reliability of this result, additional explorations included the correlation between maths and statistics anxiety so we could confirm that the use of "maths" vs "statistics" in the survey questions did not bias results. Additionally, a linear regression attempting to control for university, gender, and degree year was included. These final analyses were exploratory and do not aim to establish causation, instead ensuring that our final result still seemed reasonable when accounting for these other factors.


# Details of the Analysis
## Description of Dataset

The data is from an International Multi-Centre Study of Statistics and Mathematics Anxieties and Related Variables in University Students (the SMARVUS Dataset) [@SMARVUS_paper]. This dataset contains survey responses from 12,570 students from 100 universities in 35 countries. They attempted to measure anxieties (statistics and mathematics), collected demographics, previous mathematics grades, self-reported and official statistics grades, and statistics module details. In the following sections, we discuss the data, what we decided to include in our final analysis and our methodology.

## Data Processing

```{r load_data}
smarvus_raw <- read_csv("smarvus_complete_050524.csv",
                      show_col_types = FALSE, 
                      na = c("", "NA", "Not Available"))
```

We chose to include only universities in the UK in our analysis because this ensures that our results aren't affected by any other cultural or language-based differences between participants that could affect grades or maths anxiety. Additionally, it is the country with the most observations, at 2962, making up almost 24% of the data. Finally, all UK universities reported their grades on a percentage scale, preventing possible issues arising from different grading scales.

```{r uk_filter}
smarvus_uk <- smarvus_raw[smarvus_raw$country %in% c("England",
                                                     "Scotland",
                                                     "Northern Ireland"), ]
```
 
Six "attention checks" were built in to the survey. We used the first 3 of these to filter out any participants who weren't paying attention to questions about their statistics anxiety levels (9.18%), as this would invalidate their other responses. These attention checks were chosen as they come at the end of each section of data that was used, we did not want to exclude useable data based on checks that came after data that we did not need. People may lose attention towards the end of the survey but this does not make their early responses unreliable. Additionally, we filtered out students who responded "No" to the question "Please indicate whether you feel you have answered the previous questions carefully and truthfully" (0.91%). This was to preserve the reliability of responses.

```{r attention_checks}
smarvus_filtered <- smarvus_uk %>%
  filter(
    attention_amnesty == "Yes",
    Q7.1_24 == 1,
    Q8.1_21 == 5,
    Q9.1_22 == 1
  )

# table to check percentage of responders removed after filtering
#by attention, sequentially
seq_check_changes <- smarvus_uk %>%
  summarise(
    initial   = n(),
    amnesty   = sum(attention_amnesty == "Yes", na.rm = TRUE),
    check1    = sum(attention_amnesty == "Yes" & Q7.1_24 == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    check2    = sum(attention_amnesty == "Yes" & Q7.1_24 == 1 & Q8.1_21 == 5, 
                    na.rm = TRUE),
    check3    = sum(attention_amnesty == "Yes" & Q7.1_24 == 1 & Q8.1_21 == 5 
                    & Q9.1_22 == 1, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "decision",
    values_to = "remaining"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    excluded = lag(remaining, default = first(remaining)) - remaining
  ) %>%
  select(decision, excluded, remaining) 

replacement_decision_names <- c(
  "Initial", 
  "Amnesty Check Failed", 
  "Attention Check 1 Failed", 
  "Attention Check 2 Failed",
  "Attention Check 3 Failed"
)

seq_check_changes <- seq_check_changes %>%
  mutate(decision = replacement_decision_names)

colnames(seq_check_changes) <- c("Values Removed", "Excluded", "Remaining")

kable(seq_check_changes)
```

Additionally, we filtered our data to only include Psychology undergraduate students who were studying a statistics module. We specifically chose to filter by Psychology as the degree major, as they made up the vast majority of degree majors at the UK universities surveyed (94.5%), and this would also improve the strength of our comparisons between students, as different course demands and difficulty levels would also likely affect anxiety levels.

```{r undergrad_stats}
smarvus_psych <- smarvus_filtered %>%
  filter(
    degree_major == "Psychology"
  )

# check percentage of responders removed after filtering by degree major
seq_degree_changes <- smarvus_filtered %>%
  summarise(
    initial = n(),
    study_psychology = sum(degree_major == "Psychology", na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "decision",
    values_to = "remaining"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    excluded = lag(remaining, default = first(remaining)) - remaining
  ) %>%
  select(decision, excluded, remaining) 

replacement_decision_names <- c(
  "Initial", 
  "Non-Psychology Removed"
)

seq_degree_changes <- seq_degree_changes %>%
  mutate(decision = replacement_decision_names)

colnames(seq_degree_changes) <- c("Values Removed", "Excluded", "Remaining")

kable(seq_degree_changes)
```

### Grade Missingness

Only 20 universities in the SMARVUS data provided grade information for the statistics course participants were taking at the time of the survey, and of these, 8 were UK universities. We chose to only use university-reported grades instead of student-reported grades, for reliability. Further, this prevents any investigation of the inverse relationship (What effect does attainment have on statistics anxiety?) due to student-reported grades being for previous statistics courses as opposed to the one participants were currently enrolled on. To investigate the effect of statistics anxiety on attainment, we removed all missingness from the UK grades data, leading to 795 grade observations.

``` {r na_grades_by_degree}
# convert all percentage grades to numeric
# uk grade entries are all percentages or numeric, no letters
smarvus_clean <- smarvus_psych %>%
  mutate(grade_numeric = parse_number(grade, na = c("", "NA", 
                                                    "Not Available")))

# table of grade data by uk uni
uk_university_nas <- smarvus_clean %>%
  group_by(university) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    n_na = sum(is.na(grade_numeric)),
    n_not_na = sum(!is.na(grade_numeric))
  )

# convert to long for plotting
uk_nas_long <- uk_university_nas %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(n_not_na, n_na),
    names_to = "grade_status",
    values_to = "count"
  ) %>%
  mutate(grade_status = recode(grade_status,
                               n_not_na = "Grade present",
                               n_na = "Grade missing"))

# barplot
grade_na_byuni <- ggplot(
  uk_nas_long,
  aes(
    x = fct_reorder(
      university,
      count * (grade_status == "Grade present"),
      .fun = sum,
      .desc = TRUE),
    y = count, 
    fill = grade_status)
  ) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    title = "Grade missingness in SMARVUS by University",
    subtitle = "SMARVUS, UK Universities Psychology subset",
    x = "University", 
    y = "Number of observations", 
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(angle = 90))

grade_na_byuni
```

The degree of missingness also varied largely across degree years. The majority of students surveyed were first and second year (92%) and over half of their grade data was missing. Around 97% of grade data for students in third year was missing, while 100% of grade data for students in fourth year being missing. This could be because the only mandatory statistics courses take place in the 1st and 2nd years of students degrees and so only a few respondents have statistics module grades to report in 3rd and 4th year. As a result, it must be noted that our analysis may be less applicable to students in later years. 

```{r}
degree_nas_pct <- smarvus_clean %>%
  group_by(degree_year) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    pct_na = round(sum(is.na(grade_numeric)) / n * 100, 2)
  )

colnames(degree_nas_pct) <- c("Degree Year", "Number of Grade Observations", 
                              "Percentage of NA Grade Observations")

kable(degree_nas_pct)
```

We then investigated the distribution of reported grades to check for reliability and any possible issues with the data. The overall distribution showed that the majority lie around 65% with very few grades below ~30%. However, since this plot is the overall distribution, it may conceal differences between universities, so we also investigated the distribution of grades at each university. These were largely reasonable, apart from at the University of Southampton. The below bar graph shows their distribution of grades. This further motivates standardising the grades so that we account for some courses/universities having different grade distributions.


```{r southampton_plot, fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
# select reported grades from University of Southampton
grades_southampton <- smarvus_clean[
  !is.na(smarvus_clean$grade_numeric) &
    smarvus_clean$university == "University of Southampton",
]

southampton_plot <- ggplot(
  grades_southampton,
  aes(x = factor(grade_numeric))
) +
  geom_bar(
    fill = "steelblue3",
    colour = "white"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    stat = "count",
    aes(label = after_stat(count)),
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 3
  ) +
  ylim(0, 80) +
  labs(
    title = "Grade Distribution: University of Southampton",
    x = "Statistics Module Grade (%)",
    y = "Number of students"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8)
  )

southampton_plot
```

As we can see, almost all grades at Southampton were reported as 65%. Of the 71 participants from Southampton that were still included after our initial data preparation, 68 (95.8%) of them had an officially reported grade of 65. We additionally checked that it wasn't our data cleaning that had led to this issue, but found the same problem when including *all* University of Southampton participants with officially reported grades. This led us to conclude that the grade data from Southampton was unreliable, and perhaps 65 was some kind of placeholder value rather than a truly achieved result. The grades of the 3 other Southampton participants remaining also do not imply that this is a result of banded marking. As grade data is key to our analysis, we therefore chose to exclude the University of Southampton from our analysis.

Additionally, we also chose to exclude those with a reported grade of 0, as we believed this was likely to represent non-submission rather than a genuine attempt at an assignment, and therefore this does not give a good indication of attainment. However in our sensitivity analysis in a later section, we assess the impact of this decision, as it is possible that non-submission could be a result of extreme anxiety, and thus we could be losing information.

```{r grades_clean, fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
# removing all observations that are missing grade data (assuming missing 
#at random),
# also remove zero grades, and University of Southampton
smarvus_uk_cleangrades <- smarvus_clean %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(grade_numeric),
    grade_numeric != 0,
    university != "University of Southampton"
  )

# table to check percentage of responders removed after filtering by 
#missing grade
seq_grade_changes <- smarvus_clean %>%
  summarise(
    initial = n(),
    missing_grade = sum(!is.na(grade_numeric), na.rm = TRUE),
    zero_removed = sum(!is.na(grade_numeric) & smarvus_clean$grade_numeric 
                       != 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    southampton_removed = sum(!is.na(grade_numeric) 
                              & smarvus_clean$grade_numeric != 0
                              & smarvus_clean$university != 
                                "University of Southampton", 
                              na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "decision",
    values_to = "remaining"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    excluded = lag(remaining, default = first(remaining)) - remaining
  ) %>%
  select(decision, excluded, remaining) 

replacement_decision_names <- c(
  "Initial", 
  "Missing Grades Removed",
  "Zero Grades Removed",
  "Southampton Grades Removed"
)

seq_grade_changes <- seq_grade_changes %>%
  mutate(decision = replacement_decision_names)

colnames(seq_grade_changes) <- c("Values Removed", "Excluded", "Remaining")

kable(seq_grade_changes)
```

### Standardisation of Grades

While filtering the data to only include Psychology students at UK universities makes our analysis less susceptible to unexplained differences between students that would influence their grade or anxiety level, this does not mean that all students from this dataset can be easily compared. Even though two students may be taking similar courses, difficulty could vary across university and module. One way to make grades more comparable is standardisation against their class members. 

```{r standardisation}

smarvus_scaled <- smarvus_uk_cleangrades %>%
  group_by(grade_module_name) %>%
  mutate(
    grade_standardised = as.numeric(scale(grade_numeric))
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

smarvus_100_scale <- smarvus_scaled %>%
  mutate(
    mean_grade_overall = mean(grade_numeric),
    sd_grade_overall = sd(grade_numeric),
    grade_100 = (grade_standardised * sd_grade_overall) + mean_grade_overall
  )
N <- nrow(smarvus_100_scale)
mean_grade <- mean(smarvus_100_scale$grade_100)
```

Below we see the distribution of the grades from our final cleaned dataset with standardised grades, which has `r N` datapoints, and we can see that the majority lie around 65%. Specifically, the mean grade was `r round(mean_grade, 2)`%.

```{r grades_hist}

grades_hist <- ggplot(smarvus_100_scale, aes(x = grade_100)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)), 
    bins = 20, 
    fill = "lightgreen", 
    color = "white", 
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_density(color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Statistics Module Grades",
    subtitle = "SMARVUS, UK Universities Psychology subset",
    x = "Grade (%)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

grades_hist
```

## Statistics Anxiety

To measure statistics anxiety, the STARS (Statistics Anxiety Rating Scale) tool was used. The 3 anxiety subscales of STARS were used, giving 23 total items. Each is to be rated on a 5-point scale, with a 1 indicating "no anxiety" related to the stated item, and a 5 indicating "a great deal of anxiety". The scale includes items such as "Studying for an examination in a statistics course," and "Trying to understand the odds in a lottery." We calculated a total STARS score for each participant by summing their responses for the 23 items (ensuring we excluded the attention check question at the end of the section). The possible range for total STARS score is 23-115, with a higher score indicating greater statistics anxiety.

The distribution of STARS scores is shown below.

```{r stars_hist, fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
# find stars score for each observation
stars_totals <- smarvus_100_scale %>%
  subset(select = -c(Q7.1_24)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("Q7.1_"),
    values_to = "STARS"
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    .by = unique_id,
    stars_score = sum(STARS)
  )

# left_join with grade data
smarvus_uk_scored <- smarvus_100_scale %>%
  left_join(stars_totals, by = "unique_id")

stars_hist <- ggplot(smarvus_uk_scored, aes(x = stars_score)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)), 
    bins = 20, 
    fill = "pink", 
    color = "white", 
    alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_density(color = "deeppink4", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Statistics Anxiety Scores (STARS)",
    subtitle = "SMARVUS, UK Universities Psychology subset",
    x = "Total STARS Score (Range: 23 - 115)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

stars_hist
```

The mean STARS score was `r round(mean(smarvus_uk_scored$stars_score, na.rm = TRUE), 2)`, and the median was `r median(smarvus_uk_scored$stars_score, na.rm = TRUE)`, with a standard deviation of `r round(sd(smarvus_uk_scored$stars_score, na.rm = TRUE), 2)`. Observed scores ranged from 28 to 115. A check was carried out to ensure that partial answers to the STARS section (i.e. anyone who had answered some of the STARS questions but not all) were not included so as not to skew the sum, but no partial answers were found, so all responses were included.

## Relationship Between Statistics Anxiety and Attainment

To investigate the relationship between statistics anxiety and attainment, we looked at the association between participants' total STARS score and their grades in their statistics modules (in percentage).

Below is a scatterplot of total STARS score against statistics module grades. We can see the fitted regression line and 95% confidence interval showing the estimated statistics module grade at each STARS score. 
```{r, fig.width=5, fig.height=3}
stars_attainment <- ggplot(smarvus_uk_scored, 
                           aes(x = stars_score, y = grade_100)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "firebrick", se = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between Statistics Anxiety and Module Grades",
    subtitle = "SMARVUS, UK Universities Psychology subset",
    x = "Total STARS Score (23 - 115)",
    y = "Statistics Module Grade (%)"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(20, 100)) +
  theme_minimal()

stars_attainment
```

This plot suggests there is a weakly negative relationship between statistics anxiety and statistics module grades. The predicted grade at a STARS score of 28 is around  `r round(predict(lm(grade_100 ~ stars_score, data = smarvus_uk_scored), data.frame(stars_score = 28)))`%, while for a STARS score of 115 it is around `r round(predict(lm(grade_100 ~ stars_score, data = smarvus_uk_scored), data.frame(stars_score = 115)))`%. 

```{r}
grades_cor_result <- cor.test(smarvus_uk_scored$stars_score, 
                              smarvus_uk_scored$grade_100)

grades_d <- effectsize::r_to_d(grades_cor_result$estimate)
```

Using Pearson's correlation coefficient to measure the strength of the relationship, we found that the correlation was `r round(grades_cor_result$estimate, 2)`, with $p<0.001$ , and a 95% confidence interval of [`r round(grades_cor_result$conf.int[1], 2)`, `r round(grades_cor_result$conf.int[2], 2)`]. Taken together, these results indicate a weak but statistically significant negative relationship between statistics anxiety and attainment. 

However, due to the nature of the study, we cannot conclude whether this relationship is causal or whether other factors contributed to or explain the observed relationship.
We additionally converted the correlation coefficient into our Cohen's d effect size value, and found an effect size of `r round(grades_d, 2)` given `r N` datapoints. This had a 95% confidence interval [`r round(effectsize::r_to_d(grades_cor_result$conf.int[1]), 2)`, `r round(effectsize::r_to_d(grades_cor_result$conf.int[2]), 2)`]. As our variables are continuous, calculating Cohen's d directly from group means was not appropriate. We considered splitting participants manually into two groups ("high" and "low" anxiety), but decided against this as the splitting would be arbitrary and would result in loss of information.

The scatterplot shows no obvious outliers or curvature, so the relationship between STARS score and grade appears to be approximately linear. Both histograms are also roughly symmetric and unimodal, so neither variable is strongly skewed.  We therefore considered using Pearson's correlation to be more appropriate than Spearman's correlation. Furthermore, the conversion from a correlation r to Cohen's $d$, $d = \frac{2r}{\sqrt{1-r^2}}$, is based on Pearson's $r$, so using Spearman's correlation would only give a rough approximation. 


## Relationships Between Other Variables
After concluding our main analysis, we then performed additional exploratory analyses in order to assess the reliability of our results and check to see if other factors may influence the effect size. More specifically, we looked at alternative anxiety measures such as "statistics" vs "mathematics" anxiety scores to see whether the observed effect was specific to statistics anxiety. Additionally, we fitted a regression model to confirm that our negative relationship between anxiety and attainment remained when accounting for other variables such as university, gender, degree year, and previous mathematics education. These analyses were conducted so that we could assess the reliability of our result; however, these are exploratory and do not establish causation. 


### Alternate Anxiety Measures
We firstly examined the relationships between different measures of statistics anxiety and mathematics anxiety. This allowed us to investigate whether the phrasing of the questions was influencing the results, as well as how closely related maths and statistics anxiety were. This is particularly important as it may be difficult to distinguish the effects of each type of anxiety on attainment.

The dataset had questions used to measure statistics anxiety (stars_score) and questions used to measure maths anxiety (rmars_score). The researchers created additional measures by adapting the wording of the questions: so the statistics questions were posed again but with the word "statistics" replaced by "maths" (stars_m_score) and vice versa, so the maths questions were posed again but with the word "maths" replaced by "statistics" (rmars_s_score). 

We can see in the heatmap below that the correlations between the original and adapted measures for both statistics and maths were very high (0.86 for statistics and 0.85 for maths), suggesting the phrasing of the questions is unlikely to be biasing the results. However, there was also a strong correlation between statistics and maths anxiety (0.77 when using the original measures and 0.79 when using the adapted measures). This suggests that the two types of anxiety are closely related, which means it is hard to determine whether any relationship with attainment is specific to statistics anxiety or whether it also reflects a more general relationship with maths anxiety.

```{r, fig.width=5, fig.height=3}

# STARS Score is as calculated previously

# STARS-M Score 
stars_m_totals <- smarvus_100_scale %>%
  subset(select = -c(Q8.1_21)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("Q8.1_"),
    values_to = "STARS_M"
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    .by = unique_id,
    stars_m_score = sum(STARS_M) 
  )

# R-MARS Score 
rmars_totals <- smarvus_100_scale %>%
  subset(select = -c(Q8.2_21, Q8.2_22, Q8.2_23, Q8.2_24)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("Q8.2_"),
    values_to = "R_MARS"
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    .by = unique_id,
    rmars_score = sum(R_MARS)
  )

# R-MARS-S Score 
rmars_s_totals <- smarvus_100_scale %>%
  subset(select = -c(Q7.2_20, Q7.2_21, Q7.2_22, Q7.2_23)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("Q7.2_"),
    values_to = "R_MARS_S"
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    .by = unique_id,
    rmars_s_score = sum(R_MARS_S)
  )

# join into a single df
smarvus_all_scores <- smarvus_100_scale %>%
  left_join(stars_totals, by = "unique_id") %>%
  left_join(stars_m_totals, by = "unique_id") %>%
  left_join(rmars_totals, by = "unique_id") %>%
  left_join(rmars_s_totals, by = "unique_id")

anxiety_corrs <- smarvus_all_scores %>%
  select(stars_score, stars_m_score, rmars_score, rmars_s_score) %>%
  cor(use = "complete.obs")

cor_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(anxiety_corrs))

ggplot(cor_long, aes(Var1, Var2, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "green4", high = "firebrick", mid = "yellow2", 
                       midpoint = 0, limit = c(-1, 1), 
                       name = "Correlation (r)") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(Freq, 2)), color = "black", size = 4.5) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation Heatmap of Anxiety Measures",
    x = "", 
    y = ""
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

### Exploratory Multiple Linear Regression

The correlation and effect size found in our main analysis describe the relationship between statistics anxiety and attainment in isolation. However, grades may differ between universities, genders, degree years and levels of prior maths education, and if these characteristics are also related to STARS scores, the observed correlation could partly reflect them. We therefore decided to fit a multiple linear regression model to investigate whether the observed negative association between statistics anxiety and attainment persisted after accounting for these other variables. Since we investigated the effect on attainment, statistics module grade was used as the response variable with total STARS score as the main explanatory variable. University, gender, degree year and prior mathematics education were included as additional explanatory variables to account for potential differences in institutional context and student characteristics. The regression also allows the effect to be expressed in units that are easier to interpret (percentage points of grade per point of STARS score) and reveals how much of the variation in grades the predictors explain.


#### Exploratory Data Analysis

Before fitting a model, we examined the relationship between the chosen covariates and the response variable, as well as any relationships between them. The analysis was restricted to participants identifying as either Female/Woman or Male/Man (due to the small sample size of the "Another gender" category) and any observations with missing values for any of the model variables were excluded, leaving 783 observations.

```{r reg_eda, fig.height=9, fig.width=15}

reg_data <- smarvus_uk_scored %>%
  filter(gender %in% c("Female/Woman", "Male/Man")) %>%
  mutate(gender = factor(gender, levels = c("Female/Woman", "Male/Man"))) %>%
  drop_na(grade_100, stars_score, university, 
          gender, degree_year, math_edu_level)

covariates <- c("university", "gender", "degree_year", "math_edu_level")

make_plot <- function(var) {
  
  plot <- ggplot(reg_data, aes(x = stars_score, y = grade_100, 
                               color = .data[[var]])) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.8) +
    labs(
      title = paste("By", var),
      x = "Total STARS Score (23 - 115)",
      y = "Grade (%)",
      color = NULL
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
  
  return(plot)
}

plots <- map(covariates, make_plot)

stars_grid <- wrap_plots(plots, ncol = 2) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Statistics Anxiety vs Grade, by Covariate",
    subtitle = "SMARVUS, UK Universities Psychology subset"
  )

stars_grid
```

The university level data is noisy, and some universities have many more observations than others (for example University of Sussex), so it is difficult to make inferences from the scatterplot. However, we observed that there is a difference between grades at the same STARS scores, and the general trend of grade vs STARS score differs between universities.

The grade vs STARS score slope also differed between men and women, with women's grades decreasing at a faster rate as statistics anxiety levels increase compared to men. This could be explained by difference in approaches to anxiety and assessment between men and women, but further investigations would be required to explore this.

Noting that there is more data for first and second year students in comparison to third year students, we observed that second year students' grades decrease more as statistics anxiety increases, which could possibly be explained by an increase in difficulty between first and second year, but again, further explorations are required.

Finally, attainment vs STARS score varies by the highest level of maths education prior to university, with students who took A-Level Maths having higher grades for each STARS score in comparison to students who only took GCSE Maths.

Therefore we have evidence to include these covariates in our multiple regression model. It is also important to check for association between covariates, since strongly associated predictors can inflate the standard errors of coefficient estimates and make them difficult to interpret. To do this, we use Cramér's V, which is a measure of correlation used for categorical variables [@mchugh_2018]. Specifically, it measures the strength of the association between two categorical variables. It has a possible range of 0 to 1, with 0 indicating no association and 1 indicating a perfect association, though unlike Pearson's correlation coefficient, there is no indication of the direction of the relationship with Cramér's V. The following heatmap uses Cramér's V to show the strength of the association between the categorical predictors. 

```{r reg_cramers_v, fig.width=5, fig.height=3}

cat_vars <- c("gender", "degree_year", "math_edu_level", "university")

cv_long <- expand_grid(v1 = cat_vars, v2 = cat_vars) %>%
  mutate(cramer_v = map2_dbl(v1, v2, ~ {
    tab <- table(reg_data[[.x]], reg_data[[.y]])
    suppressWarnings(rstatix::cramer_v(tab))
    }))

cv_plot <- ggplot(cv_long, aes(v1, v2, fill = cramer_v)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "green4", high = "firebrick", mid = "yellow2", 
                       midpoint = 0.5, limit = c(0, 1), name = "Cramér's V") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(cramer_v, 2)), color = "black", size = 4.5) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Association Between Covariates (Cramér's V)",
    x = "", 
    y = ""
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

cv_plot
```

From this plot, we saw that the strongest association is between university and degree year, which indicates that the number of students in each degree year wasn't distributed the same across the universities for our data. However, none of the associations are very large, so there is no evidence of redundancy amongst the covariates, therefore we did not make any adjustment for this when creating the model. 

#### Model fitting

Our full model was
$$
\text{Grade}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{STARS}_i + \sum_{j=2}^{7} \gamma_j\,\text{Uni}_{ij} + \delta\,\text{Male}_i + \sum_{k=2}^{3} \theta_k\,\text{Year}_{ik} + \sum_{m=2}^{4} \lambda_m\,\text{MathEdu}_{im} + \varepsilon_i,$$ $$ \varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2),
$$

where $\text{Grade}_i$ is the standardised statistics module grade (%) of student $i$, $\text{STARS}_i$ is their total STARS score, and $\text{Male}_i$ is an indicator equal to 1 if the student is male and 0 if female. $\text{Uni}_{ij}$, $\text{Year}_{ik}$ and $\text{MathEdu}_{im}$ are indicator variables for university, degree year and highest level of prior mathematics education respectively, each with one reference category. The errors $\varepsilon_i$ are assumed to be independent with constant variance $\sigma^2$.

We used backward elimination to obtain a more parsimonious model. Starting with the full model, we used partial F-tests to assess each explanatory variable. At each step, the variable with the largest p-value was considered for removal, provided it was not STARS score since this was the main variable of interest.

```{r}

# Full model
lm_full <- lm(grade_100 ~ stars_score + factor(university) 
              + factor(gender) + factor(degree_year) 
              + factor(math_edu_level), data = reg_data)

# Partial F-test for backwards elimination
drop1(lm_full, test = "F")
```

Based on the partial F-test, we first removed prior mathematics education since it had the largest p-value, $0.078>0.05$. We then refitted the model without this term and did another partial F-test to examine the remaining terms.

```{r}
lm2 <- lm(grade_100 ~ stars_score + factor(university) + factor(gender) + 
            factor(degree_year), data = reg_data)

drop1(lm2, test = "F")
```

Since none of the terms have a p-value greater than 0.05, we remove no further terms from this model.

Our final model was therefore
$$
\text{Grade}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{STARS}_i + \sum_{j=2}^{7} \gamma_j\,\text{Uni}_{ij} + \delta\,\text{Male}_i + \sum_{k=2}^{3} \theta_k\,\text{Year}_{ik} + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2).
$$

```{r}
summary(lm2)

# 95% CI for STARS score
confint(lm2)["stars_score", ]
```

In this final model, STARS score was negatively associated with attainment ($\beta = -0.093, p<0.001$). This implies that, holding the other variables constant, a 10 point increase in a student's STARS score was associated with a 0.93 percentage-point decrease in statistics module grade. Furthermore, the model has an adjusted $R^2$ of 0.103, indicating that approximately 10.3% of the variation in grades was explained by our included predictors, after accounting for model complexity. This is somewhat unsurprising, as the available data provided only limited information about students previous academic attainment. In particular, prior mathematics grades were recorded inconsistently across different qualification systems, making it difficult to incorporate them reliably into the model. Consequently, potentially important sources of variation in university grades may not have been captured.

```{r residuals, fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
par(mfrow = c(2,2))
plot(lm2)
```

We also examined residual diagnostic plots to assess the assumptions of the linear regression model. These indicated slight heteroscedasticity and deviations from normality in the tails of the Q-Q plot. However, these departures were not considered sufficiently severe to invalidate the analysis. 

This suggests that the negative association between statistics anxiety and attainment observed in the Pearson correlation analysis persists after adjusting for other student characteristics. However, this still cannot establish causation.

Ultimately, for our report we have opted to use the Pearson correlation as our final stated result in Seciton 1, rather than the regression. The regression coefficient for STARS score describes the association only after adjusting for university, gender and degree year, so its value depends on which covariates are included in the model. Furthermore, it is measured in percentage points of grade per STARS point, thus, it is not a standardised effect size and can't be simply converted to Cohen's $d$. In contrast, Pearson correlation is already standardised, converts straightforwardly to $d$, and our scatterplot supports its linearity assumption. The residual diagnostics also showed slight heteroscedasticity and tail departures from normality, which added some uncertainty to the regression estimate. However, it is still important to note that the two approaches agree in direction and significance (Pearson $r$ = `r round(grades_cor_result$estimate, 2)`; regression $\beta = -0.083$, $p<0.01$), so the choice affects the precise magnitude of the effect rather than our overall conclusion.

### Sensitivity Analysis
To determine to what extent our data preparation affected our results, we carried out a sensitivity analysis. This involved repeating our main analysis many times, changing one data preparation decision at a time and calculating the resulting effect size.

The decisions we investigated were:

1. not removing those who failed one of our selected attention checks
2. removing any participant who failed any of the 7 attention checks included in the full survey
3. including those enrolled on degrees other than psychology
4. not removing those with zero as their statistics module grade
5. not removing participants from the University of Southampton

For each iteration, we recalculated the Pearson's correlation coefficient, converted it to  Cohen's d effect size, and reported a 95% confidence interval.
```{r, include = FALSE}
no_attention_base <- smarvus_uk %>%
  filter(degree_major == "Psychology") %>%
  mutate(
    grade_numeric = parse_number(
      grade,
      na = c("", "NA", "Not Available")
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(grade_numeric),
    grade_numeric != 0,
    university != "University of Southampton"
  )  %>%
  group_by(grade_module_name) %>%
  mutate(
    grade_standardised = as.numeric(scale(grade_numeric))
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    mean_grade_overall = mean(grade_numeric),
    sd_grade_overall = sd(grade_numeric),
    grade_100 = grade_standardised * sd_grade_overall +
      mean_grade_overall
  )

  subset(select = -c(Q7.1_24)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("Q7.1_"),
    values_to = "STARS"

  summarise(
    .by = unique_id,
    stars_score = sum(STARS)

datasets <- list(no_attention = no_attention,
                 not_just_psych = not_just_psych,
                 full_attention_check = full_attention_check,
                 with_zeros = no_zeros,
                 with_southampton = with_southampton, 
                 main_analysis = main_analysis)

forest_list <- lapply(names(datasets), function(name) {
  
  dat <- datasets[[name]]
  
  cor_result <- cor.test(
    dat$stars_score,
    dat$grade_standardised
  )
  
  d_est <- effectsize::r_to_d(cor_result$estimate)
  
  d_ci <- effectsize::r_to_d(
    r = cor_result$conf.int[1:2])
  
  data.frame(
    Variable = name,
    d = as.numeric(d_est),
    CI_low = as.numeric(d_ci[1]),
    CI_high = as.numeric(d_ci[2]))
})
dat <- no_standardisation

cor_result <- cor.test(
  dat$stars_score,
  dat$grade_numeric
)

d_est <- effectsize::r_to_d(cor_result$estimate)

d_ci <- effectsize::r_to_d(
  r = cor_result$conf.int[1:2])

data.frame(
  Variable = "no_standardisation",
  d = as.numeric(d_est),
  CI_low = as.numeric(d_ci[1]),
  CI_high = as.numeric(d_ci[2]))

forest_data <- do.call(rbind, forest_list)
forest_data <- rbind(
  forest_data,
  data.frame(
    Variable = "no_standardisation",
    d = as.numeric(d_est),
    CI_low = as.numeric(d_ci[1]),
    CI_high = as.numeric(d_ci[2])
  )
)

forest_data <- forest_data %>%
  mutate(Label = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]",
                    d, CI_low, CI_high))
```

```{r sensitivity analysis, fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
ggplot(forest_data,
       aes(y = Variable, x = d, xmin = CI_low, xmax = CI_high)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_errorbarh(height = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_text(aes(x = max(CI_high) + 0.25, label = Label), hjust = 0) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Effect sizes from Sensitivity Analysis",
    x = "Cohen's d", y = NULL) +
  xlim(min(forest_data$CI_low), max(forest_data$CI_high) + 0.5)

```

As we can see from the figure, all effect sizes remained largely consistent with that of our main analysis. This suggests that none of the individual data preparation decisions we made had a significant impact on our results, and that our results are robust to these alternative decisions.
